rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(a) A reaction is second order in X and first order in Y. How is the rate affected when the concentrations of both X and Y are doubled ?
(b) Write the units of 'k' for
(i) zero order reaction
(ii) first order reaction
rows.solution:
(a) The rate becomes EIGHT TIMES its original value.

The rate law follows from the orders given:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{X}]^2[\mathrm{Y}]\)

Doubling BOTH concentrations multiplies each factor by its own power of 2:
\(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = (2)^2 \times (2)^1 = 4 \times 2 = 8\)

The lesson is that the EXPONENTS multiply up, so the total effect is \(2^{\,\text{overall order}}\) — here \(2^3 = 8\), the overall order being 3.

(b) For a reaction of order \(n\) the rate constant carries the units
\(k = \dfrac{\text{Rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^n}\), that is \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

(i) ZERO ORDER: \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) — the same as the rate itself, because with no concentration term \(k\) IS the rate.

(ii) FIRST ORDER: \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) — the concentration cancels entirely, which is why a first order rate constant is a pure reciprocal time and why its half-life depends on nothing else.

rows.stem:
Out of the following pairs, predict with reason which will allow greater conduction of electricity :
(i) 1M \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) solution or 0.1M \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) solution on dilution.
(ii) Copper wire at \(27\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) or Copper wire at \(50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
rows.solution:
(i) The 0.1 M solution — the expected answer, on the ground that DILUTION INCREASES THE DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION.

Acetic acid is a WEAK electrolyte, only slightly ionised. Diluting shifts the ionisation equilibrium towards more ions, which is Ostwald's dilution law, so a larger FRACTION of each mole is ionised at 0.1 M than at 1 M — and the MOLAR conductivity, the conductance furnished per mole of electrolyte, is correspondingly higher.

Note carefully which quantity that argument is about. CONDUCTIVITY, the conductance of a fixed VOLUME, moves the other way here: the degree of dissociation rises only as \(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\), so the ion concentration itself goes as \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) and actually FALLS on dilution. The two quantities answer "greater conduction" differently, and only the per-mole one supports the expected answer.

(ii) COPPER AT \(27\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) conducts better.

Metallic conduction is carried by free ELECTRONS moving through a lattice of positive ions, and it DECREASES as the temperature rises. Heating makes the ions vibrate more violently about their positions, so they scatter the moving electrons more often and the resistance goes up.

This is the opposite of what an ELECTROLYTIC solution does, where heating speeds the ions up and raises the conductance. The two kinds of conduction respond to temperature in opposite directions, which is one way of telling them apart.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Following ions of 3d transition series are given :
\(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\),
(Atomic number : V = 23, Cr = 24, Cu = 29, Fe = 26)
Identify the ion which is
(a) unstable in aqueous solution.
(b) a strong reducing agent in aqueous solution.
(c) colourless in aqueous solution ?
Give suitable reason in each.
rows.solution:
Work out each configuration first, remembering that a transition metal loses its \(4s\) electrons before any \(3d\):
\(\mathrm{V^{3+}} = 3d^2\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}} = 3d^4\), \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}} = 3d^{10}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} = 3d^6\)

(a) UNSTABLE in aqueous solution: \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\).

It DISPROPORTIONATES, one half being oxidised and the other reduced:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

The driving force is HYDRATION ENERGY: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is smaller and doubly charged, so it is hydrated far more strongly, and that gain more than pays for the second ionisation. In the SOLID state, with no water to hydrate anything, copper(I) compounds are perfectly stable.

(b) STRONG REDUCING AGENT: \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\).

A reducing agent gives up an electron readily, and chromium(II) does, because doing so gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^3\) — in an octahedral aqueous environment the stable HALF-FILLED \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement. Its \(E^{\circ}\) is \(-0{\cdot}41\) V, negative enough that chromium(II) reduces even water.

(c) COLOURLESS in aqueous solution: \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\).

Colour arises from a D-D TRANSITION, an electron jumping from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper. Copper(I) is \(3d^{10}\) — completely FULL, with no vacancy anywhere to jump into — so no such transition is possible. The other three all have both electrons and vacancies, and are coloured.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) Transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts.
(ii) \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) is a strong reducing agent.
(iii) Chromium is hard whereas Zinc is soft metal.
rows.solution:
(i) Because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form INTERMEDIATE compounds with the reactants.

A catalyst works by offering a path of lower activation energy. A transition metal does this by accepting electrons from one reactant and passing them to another, changing oxidation state as it goes and returning to its original state at the end — so it is not consumed. Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process cycles between \(+5\) and \(+4\) in exactly this way.

Finely divided transition metals also provide a large SURFACE on which reactant molecules are adsorbed and held close together with their bonds weakened, as iron does in the Haber process.

(ii) Because \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) readily changes to the \(+3\) state, which is the characteristic state of the lanthanoids.

Giving up an electron is what a reducing agent does, and europium(II) does it easily because europium(III) is the state the whole series prefers. Europium(II) solutions therefore reduce water slowly and are oxidised by air.

(iii) Because chromium has MANY unpaired d electrons available for metallic bonding and zinc has NONE.

The hardness of a metal reflects the strength of the bond holding its lattice together, and in a transition metal the unpaired d electrons contribute to that bond alongside the \(s\) electrons. Chromium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1\) — SIX unpaired electrons, the maximum in the series — so its interatomic bonding is the strongest and the metal is very hard.

Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\). Every d electron is PAIRED and held tightly to its own atom, so only the two \(4s\) electrons take part. The bond is weak, and zinc is soft with a low melting point — mercury below it is liquid at room temperature for the same reason.

rows.stem: What is Lanthanoid contraction ? Write two consequences of Lanthanoid contraction.
rows.solution:
LANTHANOID CONTRACTION is the steady DECREASE in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series, from lanthanum to lutetium, despite the increase in atomic number.

The cause lies in the SHIELDING. Each added electron enters an inner \(4f\) orbital, and \(f\) orbitals are diffuse and poorly shaped for screening, so they shield the outer electrons from the nucleus badly. The nuclear charge rises by one at every step while the shielding barely improves, so the effective nuclear charge grows and the outer shells are pulled inwards.

The contraction is small at each step but CUMULATIVE, amounting to about 20 pm across the fourteen elements.

TWO CONSEQUENCES:

ZIRCONIUM AND HAFNIUM HAVE ALMOST IDENTICAL RADII — about 160 pm each — although hafnium lies a whole period lower, because the fourteen lanthanoids intervene between them and cancel the increase expected from the extra period. Their chemistry is so alike that they occur together and are notoriously difficult to separate.

THE LANTHANOIDS THEMSELVES ARE DIFFICULT TO SEPARATE, being so close in size and almost all in the \(+3\) state. Ion-exchange or solvent extraction, exploiting minute differences, must be used instead of ordinary chemical methods.

A third consequence worth knowing: the BASIC CHARACTER of the hydroxides decreases steadily from \(\mathrm{La(OH)_3}\) to \(\mathrm{Lu(OH)_3}\), as the shrinking ion holds the hydroxide more tightly.
